analogy.p: Imagine all the cells' DNA as a huge cookbook, and each gene as one recipe. Genetic engineering is like photocopying one recipe (isolating the gene with scissors, the restriction enzymes), cutting a slot into another cookbook (the plasmid), taping the recipe in (DNA ligase) and then giving the new cookbook to a kitchen (the bacterium) that follows it. The kitchen can read the recipe because all kitchens use the same language (the universal genetic code). The analogy breaks down because real genes are not independent recipes: where a gene is placed and how it is switched on matters, and enzymes cut at specific base sequences rather than just anywhere.
analogy.t: Genetic engineering is like copy-and-paste in a recipe book

bullets: Key definition: modifying the **genome** of an organism by **introducing a gene from another organism** to give a **desired characteristic**.
A **gene** is a short section of DNA that codes for a **protein**; the protein then produces the characteristic. So moving a gene moves the ability to make that protein.
The donor and recipient can be **different species** (even different kingdoms), because all living things use the **same genetic code**: the same base triplets code for the same amino acids.
The recipient can be a **plant, an animal or a microorganism** such as a bacterium or yeast.
The result is a **genetically modified (GM) organism**. Food from GM crops is called GM food.
Genetic engineering is different from **selective breeding**, which only reshuffles genes **already present in the same species** over many generations.
Link: genes code for proteins (Topic 4.6.1), so genetic engineering is really 'moving the instructions for one protein into a new organism'.
core.p: **Genetic engineering** is the process of **modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic**. That sentence is worth learning word for word because it is the mark-scheme definition. The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism, so changing it changes the proteins the organism can make, and therefore its characteristics. Because the gene can come from a completely different species, genetic engineering can create combinations that could never happen by normal breeding. The organism that ends up carrying the new gene is called **genetically modified (GM)** or **transgenic**.

bullets: **Universal genetic code**: a triplet such as the same three bases codes for the same amino acid in all organisms. This is why bacteria can read human genes.
**Gene expression** means the gene is transcribed and translated so that its **protein is actually made**.
A cell that has received a new gene and makes its protein is said to be **transformed**.
The new gene is copied every time the cell divides by **mitosis** (or binary fission in bacteria), so all descendant cells contain it.
Because bacteria divide very fast, one engineered bacterium can become **millions of identical cells** within hours, each making the protein.
Link: protein synthesis, so any question about how a bacterium can make a human protein should mention **the same genetic code being read by ribosomes**.
core.h: Why the same gene works in a different species
core.p: A gene works in another organism because the **genetic code is universal**: the same triplet of bases codes for the same amino acid in bacteria, plants, animals and humans. When a human insulin gene is placed in a bacterium, the bacterium's ribosomes read the gene and assemble the amino acids in exactly the right order, so it makes **human insulin**. This is called **gene expression**. Without a universal code, genetic engineering would not be possible at all. The gene also needs to be put where the cell can switch it on and copy it, which is one reason vectors are used.

bullets: The spec wording is 'enzymes are used to isolate the required gene'. Naming them as **restriction enzymes** gains extra credit and is accurate.
Restriction enzymes cut at a **specific recognition sequence** of bases, so the same enzyme always cuts in the same places.

Many restriction enzymes leave **sticky ends**: short unpaired stretches of bases. Sticky ends are useful because they can form **complementary base pairs** with other sticky ends cut by the same enzyme.
The gene must be cut out cleanly with sticky ends at **both ends** so it can be inserted the right way round.
Scientists first need to **locate the gene** on the chromosome. This is done by research and mapping; the exam will not ask you how.
Extension detail (not required by the spec): the isolated genes can be copied many times in the lab so there is plenty to use.
Exam tip: write 'enzymes cut out the gene' and 'the gene is isolated'. Do not say that the enzymes 'make' or 'create' the gene.
core.h: Stage 1 (Higher tier): isolating the required gene
core.p: The first step is to find and cut out the gene that codes for the desired characteristic. At Higher tier you must state that **enzymes are used to isolate the required gene**. The enzymes used are **restriction enzymes**, which cut DNA at **specific base sequences**. Each restriction enzyme recognises one particular sequence, so it cuts the DNA in a predictable place. The cut often leaves short single-stranded ends called **sticky ends** that can pair with matching sticky ends. The aim is to cut the DNA on **both sides of the gene** so that the gene is released as a separate fragment.

bullets: **Vector** = something that carries the gene into the new cell. Spec: 'usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus'.
A **plasmid** is a small **circular** piece of DNA in bacteria, easy to remove, cut and put back.
The plasmid is cut with the **same enzyme** as the gene, so the **sticky ends are complementary** and the gene can fit.
**DNA ligase** joins the gene into the plasmid by sealing the DNA backbone (extension detail but standard).
The plasmid containing the new gene is called a **recombinant plasmid** (recombinant DNA = DNA from two different sources joined together).
A **virus** can be used as a vector because viruses naturally insert their own genetic material into host cells.
Exam trap: a vector is **not** a disease-carrying organism in this context (as in mosquito vectors) but a **DNA carrier**.
core.p: The isolated gene cannot get into a cell by itself, so it is inserted into a **vector**. A **vector** is a carrier that transfers DNA into another cell. The AQA specification states that the vector is **usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus**. A **plasmid** is a small, circular loop of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome. To insert the gene, the plasmid is cut open with the **same restriction enzyme**, so its sticky ends match the sticky ends of the gene. The gene fits into the gap and an enzyme called **DNA ligase** joins the sugar-phosphate backbones, sealing the DNA. The plasmid is now **recombinant**, because it contains DNA from two sources.

bullets: Gene transfer is done at an **early stage of development** (for example a fertilised egg, an embryo or a young plant cell).
As the organism develops by **mitosis**, every new cell receives a copy of the gene, so the whole organism has the new characteristic.
For **plants**, the gene can be put into individual plant cells that are then grown into whole plants (the cells are totipotent, like stem cells).
For **bacteria**, the recombinant plasmid is taken into the cell and the bacterium then divides to make a **clone** of GM bacteria.
For **animals**, the gene is injected into a fertilised egg or early embryo; the animal then develops with the characteristic.
Not every cell takes up the new DNA, so scientists need ways to pick out the cells that did (not required by the spec).
Higher tier answer chain to learn: **enzymes isolate gene, gene inserted into vector (plasmid or virus), vector inserts gene into target cells at an early stage of development**.
core.h: Stage 3: inserting the vector into the cells
core.p: The vector is now used to insert the gene into the required cells. A bacterium takes up the plasmid, or a virus injects its modified DNA into the host cell. The spec says that **genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with desired characteristics**. This matters because if the gene is inserted when the organism is a single cell or a tiny embryo, then as the organism grows by mitosis **every cell** will contain the new gene. Inserting the gene into an adult would only change a few cells and the characteristic would not appear throughout the organism.

bullets: Step 1: **locate and cut out** the gene using enzymes (restriction enzymes) so it is **isolated**.
Step 2: **cut open the vector** (plasmid) with the same enzyme, leaving complementary sticky ends.
Step 3: **join the gene to the vector** (DNA ligase) to make a recombinant plasmid.
Step 4: the vector **carries the gene into the target cells** (bacterium, plant or animal cell).
Step 5: the cells **divide by mitosis**; the gene is copied; the cells make the **protein** coded for by the gene.
Step 6: the GM organisms are grown, screened and used (food, medicine, farming).
Marking tip: for 'describe how', give the steps in order. For 'explain why', add the reason after each step.
core.h: The whole sequence as a flow chart
core.p: Most 4 to 6 mark questions on this topic want the steps in the **correct order** with the **purpose** of each. The sequence is: identify and isolate the gene with enzymes; cut the vector with the same enzyme; join the gene into the vector; use the vector to insert the gene into the target cells (early in development); the cells divide and the gene is expressed. Always link each step to its reason, for instance 'the same enzyme is used so the sticky ends are complementary'. A flow chart in the notes (see the diagrams) helps you memorise it.

bullets: Treats **diabetes**: Type 1 diabetics need insulin injections because the pancreas does not make enough.
Human gene for insulin is put into **bacterial plasmids**; bacteria divide quickly, giving huge amounts of insulin cheaply.
The insulin is **identical to human insulin**, so it is less likely to cause an immune reaction than animal insulin.
Production is **large scale, fast and reliable**, and avoids using animal organs, which some people object to.
The bacteria are grown in a **fermenter** under controlled conditions (temperature, pH, nutrients, oxygen).
The insulin must be **extracted and purified** from the bacteria and the broth before use.
Other medicines made this way include **growth hormone**.
Link to homeostasis: insulin lowers blood glucose by causing glucose to move into cells and be stored as glycogen (Topic 4.5).
core.h: Example 1: bacteria that make human insulin
core.p: Bacterial cells may be engineered to produce **useful substances such as human insulin to treat diabetes**. People with Type 1 diabetes cannot make enough insulin, so they must inject it. The human gene for insulin is cut out, inserted into a bacterial plasmid, and the plasmid is put into bacteria. The bacteria are grown in huge tanks called **fermenters**, where they multiply and make **human insulin**, which is then harvested, purified and sold. This is better than the old method of extracting insulin from the pancreases of pigs and cattle, which was not an exact match for human insulin.

bullets: **Disease resistance**: a gene that protects against a virus, fungus or insect pest is inserted, so fewer crops are lost and less pesticide is needed.
**Bigger or better fruits/higher yield**: genes that improve size, shelf-life or nutrient content give more food from the same land.
Example (extension): **Bt crops** contain a bacterial gene for a toxin that kills certain insect pests but not people.
Example (extension): **Golden rice** has genes added so the grain contains **beta-carotene**, which the body converts to vitamin A. This aims to prevent vitamin A deficiency.
Example (extension): **herbicide-resistant** crops survive weedkiller, allowing farmers to kill weeds without killing the crop.
Benefits: **increased yield**, so more food from the same area; less pest damage; potentially **fewer pesticides** sprayed; crops can be given extra nutrients.
GM crops can help **food security**, i.e. feeding a growing world population, which is the argument you should make in evaluation questions.
core.p: Plant crops have been genetically engineered to be **resistant to diseases or to produce bigger, better fruits**. The spec names these two aims, and you should be able to give a developed example of each. A gene for **resistance to a pest, virus or herbicide** can be taken from another organism and put into the crop, while genes affecting **fruit size, yield or nutrition** can improve quality. GM crops are widely grown in some countries (such as the USA and Brazil) but more strictly controlled in the UK and the EU.

bullets: **Wild flowers and insects**: a GM crop that kills insect pests could also harm **harmless or beneficial insects** (such as bees), which affects **food chains** and reduces **biodiversity**.
Herbicide-resistant crops allow heavy spraying, which can kill **wild plants (weeds)** that insects depend on.
Genes may **spread to wild plants** through pollen (cross-pollination), creating herbicide-resistant 'superweeds'.
Some people worry that eating GM food **may be harmful to human health**, for example by causing allergies. This has **not been proven** and GM foods are tested before approval.
Pests can **evolve resistance** to the toxin, by natural selection, making the GM crop less useful over time.
Economic concerns: **GM seeds are expensive**, and companies may own them (patents), so farmers have to buy seed every year.
Ethical concerns: some people feel it is wrong to **interfere with nature** or to move genes between species.
In evaluation answers, give **at least one benefit and one concern**, then a conclusion that says which you think outweighs the other and why.
core.p: Not everyone supports GM crops, and you need to know the concerns the spec lists. The spec says there are concerns about the **effect on populations of wild flowers and insects**, and that **some people feel that eating GM crops may be harmful to human health**. You must be careful with wording: the harm to health is a **concern, not a proven fact**. Mark schemes reward answers that are balanced and use words like 'may', 'could' and 'some people believe'. You should also be able to link ideas to wider issues such as cost and who owns the seeds.

bullets: Selective breeding: **slow** (many generations), uses **existing variation**, many genes change at once, may reduce variation and cause **inbreeding** problems.
Genetic engineering: **fast** (one generation), changes a **single targeted gene**, gene can come from **a different species**.
Both are ways humans change organisms to give desired characteristics.
Both can produce organisms that are **genetically less varied** than wild populations, which risks disease wiping them out.
Selective breeding produces organisms by sexual reproduction, so offspring show variation; GM organisms can then be bred or cloned to spread the new gene.
Natural selection (environment chooses) differs from both: the selecting factor is **humans** in the other two.
Link: cloning (4.6.2.4, triple) can be used afterwards to make many identical copies of a successful GM organism.
core.h: Genetic engineering compared with selective breeding
core.p: Examiners often ask how genetic engineering differs from **selective breeding**. In selective breeding, humans choose parents with the desired trait and breed them over **many generations**, so you only ever use **alleles that already exist in that species**. Genetic engineering is much **faster and more precise**: a single gene is added in one generation, and it can come from any species. However, genetic engineering is more expensive, needs specialist equipment, and raises more **ethical and safety concerns**.

bullets: **Farmers**: higher yields and less crop loss, but GM seed costs more.
**Consumers**: potentially cheaper food or healthier food (more vitamins), but some are concerned about safety and want GM food labelled.
**Environment**: fewer pesticides may be needed, but there may be harm to non-target insects, wild plants and biodiversity.
**Medicine**: cheap, safe, pure human proteins like insulin, which saves lives.
**Society**: debates about who owns the technology, whether it helps developing countries, and whether it is natural.
Evidence matters: scientists run **trials**, results are **peer reviewed**, and regulators decide whether a GM product is approved.
A strong 6-mark conclusion makes a **judgement** such as 'benefits outweigh risks if properly regulated' and gives a reason.
core.h: Benefits and risks: wider issues and evaluation
core.p: A top-grade evaluation looks at **different groups of people** and weighs short-term against long-term effects. Think about farmers, consumers, the environment, and medicine. You should also state that decisions are made by society using **evidence**, and that long-term effects may not be known yet. Use comparative words (more, less, greater) and always link a point to its consequence, for example 'higher yield, so more food, so less hunger'.

bullets: **State what is meant by genetic engineering** (2 marks): 'changing/modifying the genome of an organism' + 'by introducing a gene from another organism' (for a desired characteristic).
**Describe how a gene is transferred** (up to 4 marks): enzymes isolate gene; inserted into a vector (plasmid/virus); vector inserts into the cell; early in development.
**Explain why bacteria can make human insulin** (3 marks): human insulin gene inserted into the bacteria; same genetic code, so read correctly; bacteria divide rapidly giving lots of insulin.
**Evaluate GM crops** (6 marks): at least two benefits and two concerns, a link of each to a consequence, and a final judgement.
Never say GM food 'is dangerous'. Say it 'may' have effects on health and that this is a concern.
Use scientific words: **genome, gene, vector, plasmid, enzymes, characteristic, resistant**.
If the question gives data (yields, costs), quote at least one figure in your answer.
core.h: Command words and how to answer
core.p: The command word tells you how many ideas and what kind of idea to write. For **'state'** or **'give'**, a single fact is enough. For **'describe'**, give a sequence or facts with no reasons. For **'explain'**, add 'because' reasoning. For **'evaluate'** or **'discuss'**, you need a balanced argument with both sides and a justified conclusion. Genetic engineering questions typically come as a 2 mark definition, a 4 mark 'describe how', or a 6 mark evaluation of GM crops.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark)**: one fact only, e.g. 'a plasmid' or 'a virus' for a vector. No need to explain.
**Definition (2 marks)**: 'modifying the genome of an organism' (1) 'by introducing a gene from another organism' (1). Add 'to give a desired characteristic'.

**Describe how a gene is transferred (3 to 4 marks)**: 1 enzymes isolate/cut out the gene; 2 gene inserted into a vector (plasmid or virus); 3 vector used to put the gene into the target cells; 4 at an early stage of development so all cells have it.
**Explain (2 to 3 marks)**: give a statement then 'because' or 'so', e.g. 'Bacteria divide rapidly, so large amounts of insulin are made quickly'.

**Evaluate GM crops (6 marks)**: two or more benefits (yield, disease resistance, nutrition), two or more concerns (wild flowers, insects, health, cost), consider different groups, finish with a justified conclusion. Structure: benefits paragraph, concerns paragraph, conclusion.
Use **hedging language** for unproven claims: 'may', 'could', 'some people believe'.
Higher tier only: the enzyme-and-vector detail is HT. In a Foundation-style question, defining and giving examples is enough.
**Use the data**: if a table of crop yields or pesticide use is given, compare actual numbers and state the difference, then link to a benefit.
**Compare** questions need a comparative word on both sides: 'Genetic engineering is faster, whereas selective breeding takes many generations'.
Link to other topics: proteins and enzymes (Topic 4.2), DNA structure (4.6), selective breeding (4.6.2.2) and cloning (4.6.2.4).

mistakes.r: That is selective breeding. Genetic engineering is changing the genome by introducing a gene from another organism.
mistakes.w: Genetic engineering is when you breed the best animals together.

mistakes.r: Enzymes cut out (isolate) the existing gene and join it in; they do not create it.
Some people feel that eating GM crops may be harmful to health; this is a concern and is not proven.
mistakes.w: GM food is harmful and causes illness.

mistakes.r: In genetic engineering a vector is a carrier (plasmid or virus) that transfers a gene into a cell.
mistakes.w: A vector is an organism that spreads disease.

mistakes.r: Genes are transferred to cells at an early stage in development so the organism develops with the characteristic, and all cells get it.
mistakes.w: The gene is added to the bacterium when it is fully grown.

mistakes.r: Because the human insulin gene is inserted and the genetic code is universal, so the bacteria's ribosomes can read it.
mistakes.w: Bacteria can make human insulin because they are like humans.

mistakes.r: They could affect populations of wild flowers and insects; say 'may' and name the effect on the food web or biodiversity.
mistakes.w: GM crops will definitely kill wild insects.

mistakes.r: Plasmids are small circular DNA loops found in bacteria (separate from the chromosome).
mistakes.w: Plasmids are found in the nucleus of animal cells.

summary: AQA wants you to define **genetic engineering** (changing an organism's genome by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic), give examples in crops and bacteria (human insulin), and at Higher tier describe the steps: enzymes isolate the gene, it is inserted into a vector (plasmid or virus), and the vector carries it into the target cells. You must also weigh up benefits and concerns about GM crops. It matters because it is a standard 6-mark 'evaluate' topic and links to proteins, enzymes and selective breeding.

terms.d: Modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
A short section of DNA that codes for a protein.
An organism whose genome has been altered by genetic engineering, so it contains a gene from another organism.
A carrier used to insert a gene into another cell; usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus.
A small circular loop of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome, often used as a vector.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific sequence of bases, used to isolate a gene and to cut open a plasmid.
Short unpaired single-stranded ends left by some restriction enzymes, which can pair with complementary sticky ends.
An enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone.
DNA formed by joining DNA from two different sources.
The process in which a gene is used to make its protein.
Humans breeding plants or animals for particular genetic characteristics, using alleles already in the species.
A large tank in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions to make a product, such as insulin.
A crop that is not damaged by a particular pest, disease or herbicide because of a gene it contains.
The variety of different species living in an area; a concern is that GM crops may reduce it.

worked.ans: Genetic engineering is modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
worked.q: State what is meant by genetic engineering. (2 marks)
steps: Mark 1: modifying the genome of an organism.
Mark 2: by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.

worked.ans: Enzymes isolate the insulin gene. The gene is inserted into a vector, which is a bacterial plasmid. The vector inserts the gene into the bacterial cell. The bacteria then divide to make many copies and produce human insulin.
worked.q: Describe how a human gene for insulin can be inserted into a bacterium. (4 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Enzymes (restriction enzymes) are used to cut out/isolate the human insulin gene.
The same enzyme cuts open a bacterial plasmid (the vector), leaving matching sticky ends.
The gene is inserted into the plasmid and joined with ligase to give a recombinant plasmid.
The plasmid (vector) is put into the bacterial cell; the bacterium divides, copying the gene and making human insulin.

worked.ans: GM crops can have higher yields and resistance to disease, so more food is produced from the same land and less is lost, which could reduce hunger. They can also be bigger or more nutritious. However, they may affect populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people believe eating them may harm health, although this is not proven. Overall, I think the benefits outweigh the concerns as long as GM crops are tested and regulated, because the need for food is great and the risks to health are unproven.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of genetically modified crops for food production. (6 marks)
steps: Benefit 1: crops can be given resistance to disease/pests, so less crop is lost and yields rise, which helps feed more people.
Benefit 2: crops can be made to produce bigger or more nutritious fruit, so better quality and less pesticide may be needed.
Concern 1: the crop may affect wild flowers and insects, for example by harming insects that are not pests, which would reduce biodiversity.
Concern 2: some people feel that eating GM crops may be harmful to health, though this is not proven.
